Registration is optional: copyright arises automatically on creation, but the Register of Copyrights under s.44–45 provides prima facie evidence of the particulars entered (s.48). Applications are made to the Registrar of Copyrights with the prescribed fee, and for artistic works used on goods, a no-objection from the Trade Marks Registry is needed. Example: a software firm registers its code to make infringement suits easier to prove.

Under s.17, the author is the first owner, with exceptions: works made by an employee under a contract of service belong to the employer; for a photograph, painting or cinematograph film made for valuable consideration at someone's instance, that person owns it; government works belong to the Government; and for literary works by journalists under employment, the proprietor owns rights for publication in newspapers. Example: software written by a Tabsyst employee in the course of employment belongs to Tabsyst absent a contrary agreement.

Under ss.18–19, the owner may assign copyright wholly or partially, for the whole or part of its term, in writing signed by the assignor, identifying the rights, territory and duration. If the duration is not stated it is deemed five years, and if the territory is not stated it is deemed India (s.19(5)–(6)). An assignment not exercised within one year lapses unless otherwise agreed (s.19(4)). Authors of works in films and sound recordings retain an equal share of royalties from non-film exploitation (s.18 proviso). Example: an app design assigned without stating duration reverts after five years.

Under ss.22–29, copyright in literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works lasts for the author's lifetime plus 60 years. For cinematograph films, sound recordings, photographs, anonymous and pseudonymous works, posthumous works, government works and works of international organisations, the term is 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following publication. Example: a novel by an author who died in 2000 remains protected until the end of 2060.

The owner can grant voluntary licences in writing (s.30). Compulsory licences are available for works withheld from the public (s.31), for unpublished or orphan works (s.31A), for persons with disabilities (s.31B), statutory licences for cover versions (s.31C) and for broadcasting of literary and musical works and sound recordings (s.31D), and for translations and reproductions (s.32, s.32A). Copyright societies under s.33 administer licensing collectively. Example: a radio station can broadcast published songs under a s.31D statutory licence by paying royalty fixed by the Commercial Court/authority.

Infringement under s.51 occurs when a person without licence does an act exclusively reserved to the owner, or permits a place for profit for infringing performance, or sells, distributes or imports infringing copies. Fair dealing for private use, research, criticism, review and reporting is exempt under s.52. Civil remedies (s.55) include injunction, damages and accounts; criminal offences under s.63 carry imprisonment of six months to three years and fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. Example: distributing pirated copies of licensed accounting software is both civil and criminal infringement.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a work protected under s.13 of the Copyright Act?
options: A bare idea for a mobile game
quiz.explain: Copyright protects expression, not ideas; s.13 covers literary, artistic and other specified works.

quiz.q: What is the legal effect of registering a copyright?
options: Entries are prima facie evidence of particulars
It extends the term by ten years
quiz.explain: Under s.48, the Register of Copyrights is prima facie evidence; copyright exists without registration.

quiz.q: A salaried developer writes code during employment without any contrary agreement. Who is the first owner?
quiz.explain: Under s.17(c), works made in the course of employment under a contract of service belong to the employer.

quiz.q: An assignment deed is silent on duration. The assignment is deemed to be for:
quiz.explain: Section 19(5) deems the duration as five years if not specified.

quiz.q: An author of a novel died in 2010. Copyright in the novel expires at the end of:
quiz.explain: Under s.22, the term is life plus 60 years from the beginning of the year following death.

quiz.q: A college copies an entire textbook and sells copies to students. Is this protected as fair dealing under s.52?
options: Yes, as it is for education
No, wholesale commercial copying is infringement under s.51
Yes, if the author is foreign
quiz.explain: Commercial reproduction and sale of entire works is an infringement under s.51 and not fair dealing.

desc.q: CodeWorks Pvt Ltd engaged a freelance designer to create its logo and app UI and engaged an employee to write the app's source code. Later, the freelancer claimed ownership of the UI and a rival sold copies of the app. Advise CodeWorks under the Copyright Act 1957.
points: The source code is a literary work (s.2(o), s.13) and, made by an employee in the course of employment, is owned by CodeWorks under s.17(c).

A freelancer is not an employee; unless there is a written assignment under ss.18–19, the freelancer owns the UI and logo, so CodeWorks should obtain a signed assignment specifying rights, territory and duration.
Registration under s.45 is optional but gives prima facie evidence under s.48 and helps in litigation.
Selling copies of the app infringes under s.51; CodeWorks can seek injunction, damages and accounts under s.55 and prosecute under s.63.

notes.note: Under s.11 of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999, any association of persons, producers, organisation or authority representing the interests of producers of the goods may apply to the Registrar of GIs at Chennai. The application must describe the goods, the geographical area, the special characteristics attributable to that origin and the method of production; GIs are classified by the Fourth Schedule classes. After examination and advertisement, any person may oppose within three months (extendable by one month) under s.14. Producers of registered GI goods may separately register as authorised users (s.17). Example: Malabar Pepper and Aranmula Kannadi are registered GIs from Kerala.

Under s.18, registration of a GI is valid for ten years and may be renewed for further periods of ten years each on payment of the renewal fee. An authorised user's registration is also for ten years or until the GI's registration lapses, whichever is earlier. If not renewed, the GI may be removed from the register after notice. Example: Darjeeling Tea, registered in 2004, must be renewed every ten years to remain on the register.

Under s.21, registration gives the registered proprietor and authorised users the right to obtain relief for infringement, and gives authorised users the exclusive right to use the GI on the goods. A GI is not assignable, transmissible, licensable or capable of being pledged (s.24), being a public property of producers. Section 22 defines infringement, including use suggesting false origin and unfair competition; s.22(2) offers additional protection for notified goods like wines and spirits. Offences of falsifying GIs are punishable under s.39 with imprisonment of six months to three years. Example: selling tea grown in Assam as 'Darjeeling Tea' infringes the GI.

A trade mark identifies goods of a particular enterprise and is owned by an individual or company, freely assignable, and renewable indefinitely. A GI identifies goods as originating from a particular territory whose quality or reputation is due to that origin, is collectively owned by producers of the area, and cannot be assigned or licensed. Section 25 bars registration of a trade mark that contains a GI where the goods do not originate from that territory and the use would mislead. Example: 'Tata Tea' is a trade mark, while 'Nilgiri Tea' is a GI usable by all authorised producers of the Nilgiris.

quiz.q: Who may apply for registration of a GI under s.11?
options: Any individual trader anywhere in India
An association of producers representing their interests
quiz.explain: Section 11 permits any association of persons, producers or authority representing producers to apply.

quiz.q: For how long is a registered GI valid before renewal?
quiz.explain: Section 18 provides registration for ten years, renewable for ten years each.

quiz.q: A registered GI proprietor wishes to sell its GI to a multinational. Under s.24 this is:
options: Not allowed, as a GI is not assignable
quiz.explain: Section 24 prohibits assignment, transmission, licensing, pledge or mortgage of a GI.

quiz.q: A company in Mumbai sells shawls made locally as 'Kashmir Pashmina'. This most likely constitutes:
options: Infringement of the GI under s.22
quiz.explain: Section 22 treats use suggesting false geographical origin as infringement.

quiz.q: Which is a key difference between a GI and a trade mark?
options: A GI is owned by one company
A trade mark cannot be renewed
A GI identifies goods from a territory and is collectively used
A trade mark is not assignable
quiz.explain: A GI denotes territorial origin and is used collectively by authorised producers, unlike a trade mark.

quiz.q: Where is the Geographical Indications Registry located?
quiz.explain: The GI Registry operates from Chennai under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.

desc.q: A group of handloom weavers in Kerala wants to protect the name of their traditional saree. A large textile company already sells sarees under a similar-sounding brand made in Gujarat. Advise the weavers under the GI Act 1999.
points: An association representing the weavers can apply under s.11 to the GI Registry, Chennai, describing the saree, geographical area, special characteristics and production process.
After examination and advertisement, opposition may be filed under s.14; on registration, individual weavers may register as authorised users under s.17.
Registration is valid for ten years and renewable (s.18); the GI cannot be assigned or licensed (s.24).

Once registered, they can sue the company for infringement under ss.21–22 for misleading use of the GI, and under s.25 oppose or seek removal of a trade mark that contains the GI for goods not originating in the area; criminal action lies under s.39.

notes.note: Under s.5 of the Designs Act 2000, the proprietor of a new or original design not previously published may apply to the Controller for registration in one or more classes (Locarno-based classification). A design means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to an article, judged solely by the eye, excluding mode of construction, trade marks and artistic works (s.2(d)). Registration gives copyright in the design for ten years from the registration date, extendable once by five years (s.11). Example: the distinctive shape of a perfume bottle can be registered as a design.

Section 4 prohibits registration of a design that is not new or original, has been disclosed to the public anywhere in India or elsewhere by publication or use before the filing or priority date, is not significantly distinguishable from known designs or combinations, or comprises scandalous or obscene matter. Designs contrary to public order or morality are also refused. Example: a chair design already sold in Malaysia before the Indian filing cannot be registered as it lacks novelty.

Upon registration the proprietor obtains 'copyright in the design', meaning the exclusive right to apply the design to any article in the class registered (s.2(c), s.11). Under s.15 of the Copyright Act 1957, copyright does not subsist in a design registered under the Designs Act, and if a design capable of registration is not registered, copyright ceases once an article with that design is reproduced more than fifty times by an industrial process. Example: an artist's unregistered textile print loses copyright protection once the owner mass-produces over 50 printed fabrics.

Piracy of a registered design under s.22 includes applying the design or a fraudulent or obvious imitation to any article in the registered class for sale without the proprietor's consent, or importing or selling such articles knowingly. The proprietor may claim up to ₹25,000 per contravention as a contract debt, with the total for one design capped at ₹50,000, or sue for damages and an injunction. Suits lie in a court not below a District Court, and the defendant may plead cancellation grounds under s.19 as a defence. Example: a factory copying a registered bottle shape for its own perfumes commits piracy.

quiz.q: For how long does copyright in a registered design subsist in total, including extension?
quiz.explain: Under s.11 Designs Act, the term is ten years, extendable once by five years.

quiz.q: Which of the following can be registered as a design?
options: The ornamental shape of a lamp
quiz.explain: Section 2(d) covers shape, pattern or ornament judged by the eye, excluding construction methods and trade marks.

quiz.q: A designer showcased a new sofa design at an exhibition abroad before filing in India. The design is likely:
options: Not registrable for lack of novelty under s.4
Registrable as foreign disclosure does not count
quiz.explain: Section 4 bars designs disclosed to the public in India or elsewhere before the filing date, subject to limited exhibition exceptions.

quiz.q: An unregistered artistic design is reproduced industrially on 60 articles. What happens to its copyright?
options: It continues for life plus 60 years
It ceases under s.15(2) of the Copyright Act
quiz.explain: Section 15(2) Copyright Act ends copyright once a registrable design is industrially reproduced more than 50 times.

quiz.q: What is the maximum amount a proprietor can recover as a contract debt for piracy of one design?
quiz.explain: Section 22(2) caps recovery at ₹25,000 per contravention and ₹50,000 in total for one design.

quiz.q: In a piracy suit, the defendant may plead which defence?
options: Any ground on which registration may be cancelled under s.19
That the plaintiff is a foreigner
That he sold fewer than 50 articles
That the design is registered as a trade mark
quiz.explain: Section 22(3) allows the defendant to rely on s.19 cancellation grounds as a defence.

desc.q: StyleCraft registered the design of a uniquely shaped water bottle in 2022. A competitor is selling bottles of an almost identical shape and claims StyleCraft's design was published on its website before filing. Advise StyleCraft under the Designs Act 2000.
points: StyleCraft's registration gives it copyright in the design under s.11 for ten years, extendable by five, and the exclusive right to apply it to articles in the registered class.
The competitor's sale of an obvious imitation for sale amounts to piracy under s.22(1).
StyleCraft may claim up to ₹25,000 per contravention (maximum ₹50,000 for the design) or sue for damages and injunction in a court not below a District Court.

The competitor may defend by alleging prior publication, a s.19 cancellation ground; if StyleCraft's website disclosure predates filing, the registration may be cancelled, so it should establish the true dates of disclosure.
